To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the association between physical and psychosocial work demands and self-rated health is not explained by socioeconomic factors.

the physical and psychosocial job demands and job control are important determinants of the self-rated health in the general working population, and that these factors are also important explanations for the occupational class inequalities in the self-rated health.

(1) physical and psychosocial work characteristics were associated with the risk of reporting poor health; (2) the association between psychosocial work and self-rated health is partly mediated by health behaviors; (3) the associations between psychosocial working condition and health were partly explained by health behaviors and social position; (4) the association between physical working conditions and self-rated health was partly mediated by social position.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how social inequalities in health are produced.
the relationship between social class and mental illness, particularly schizophrenia.
the question of why the social class gap in health has not narrowed in recent decades.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence for a causal relationship between physical and psychosocial work conditions and self-rated health is strong, but that there are also indications that the effects of psychosocial work factors are stronger than those of physical work conditions.
the physical work environment and work organization are important factors in explaining the association between occupational class and self-rated health.
there is a strong and consistent association between self-rated health and social class.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the importance of the psychosocial work environment as an explanation for occupational class inequalities, but that the importance of the physical work environment is less clear.
we have found that working conditions are important explanations for occupational class differences in health.

the physical working conditions and psychosocial factors are important explanations for the observed occupational class differences in self-rated health, and that the physical and psychosocial exposures are related to each other.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social and physical environment is a key factor for the health of older adults, but that the social environment may be more important than the physical environment.
the relationship between social class and health is not simply a function of the social environment, but also of the physical and psychosocial work environment.
the relationship between work and health can be complex, and the impact of work on health is not always straightforward.
